title: Ohm's law and power
body: Think of voltage as the push, current as the flow, and resistance as a narrow pipe. Ohm's law links all three: V = I × R. On 9 V, a 10 Ω resistor lets through 100 times the current of a 1 kΩ one.
Power is how fast the resistor turns electrical energy into heat: P = V × I. Put the two laws together and you get P = V² ÷ R. So on a fixed voltage, the lower-value resistor gets far hotter.
In a series chain it's the other way round. The same current flows through each resistor. Then P = I² × R, so the larger value runs hotter.
Every resistor has a power rating: the most heat it can safely handle. For small resistors, 0.25 W is common. Push past it and the resistor overheats and can fail.
realWorld: Circuit designers check each resistor's power against its rating. That way nothing overheats, even when the device runs at full power.
